conceptTag: A brewery partners with a restaurant
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소규모 양조장과 호텔 레스토랑, 인테리어 디자이너와 도장업체) · 실제 기업이나 수치 없음
insight: 파트너십의 성패는 계약서가 아니라 상대 쪽에서 실제로 결정을 내리는 사람이 무엇으로 평가받는지에 달려 있다.
misconception: 좋은 제품과 서로 이익이 되는 계약만 있으면 파트너가 알아서 열심히 팔아 준다. 독점을 원하면 통째로 주거나 거절하거나 둘 중 하나다.

sources.text: 모든 인물, 업체, 조건은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 실제 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 가격 구간, 기간(12개월), 거리(2km), 수수료(10%, 15%)는 모두 설명용 가상 조건입니다. 특정 국가의 주류 유통 규제(양조장-소매점 관계 제한 등)에 따라 실제로는 일부 조건이 허용되지 않을 수 있으므로, 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않는지 검토가 필요합니다.
이 레슨은 SAL-07-03(인센티브 정렬)과 SAL-07-05(독점)를 적용합니다. 수익 배분(SAL-07-04)은 3번 선택지에 간접적으로만 등장하며, 형제 레슨과 겹치지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The house beer nobody ordered
body: Hana runs a small brewery. The restaurant inside a busy downtown hotel agreed to pour her pale ale as its "house beer", with its name on the tap.
Everyone was excited at the launch. Six weeks later, the first keg was still half full. The beer was good. The deal was fair. So what went wrong?

image.label: A lonely beer tap beside a busy cocktail bar
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 호텔 레스토랑 바. 바텐더들이 칵테일을 바쁘게 만드는 동안, 한쪽 끝의 맥주 탭 하나에만 먼지 같은 작은 거미줄과 반쯤 찬 케그 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How do you get the beer moving?
body: Hana learns something over coffee with Marco, the restaurant manager. His bonus from the hotel group depends on his drinks margin. Cocktails earn him more per glass, so his servers are coached to suggest cocktails first.

options.text: Cut the keg price by 15% across the board
options.feedback: This improves Marco's margin, so it speaks to his scorecard. But Hana pays for every keg, even if sales stay flat, and nothing pushes servers to suggest the beer.

options.text: Offer a lower price that kicks in as volume grows, plus a staff tasting and a monthly server prize
options.feedback: This is **aligning incentives**: Marco's margin improves only as more beer sells, and the servers who make the suggestion now gain from it too.

options.text: Go over Marco's head to the hotel group's drinks director
options.feedback: She might win an order from head office. But Marco still controls the menu and the servers, and now he has a reason to resent the beer.

cards.title: The deal was agreed. The incentives weren't.
body: Hana's first deal made sense on paper: a fixed keg price, a tap with her name. But nobody on the restaurant side gained when a pint sold. Marco's scorecard pointed to cocktails. Servers followed Marco.

Once the volume tiers started, every extra keg lowered Marco's cost per pint. The tasting gave servers a story to tell, and the prize gave them a reason to tell it. Within two months, the beer was the second-best seller on tap.

cards.title: You partner with a company. People make the choices.
body: **Aligning incentives** means shaping a deal so each person who makes a daily decision gains when the partnership succeeds.
Inside a larger company, this is easy to miss. Marco isn't the hotel. He's a team leader judged on numbers set by someone else. Before you sign, ask: *who decides, and what are they measured on?*

image.label: Chain of decision-makers from brewery to customer
image.brief: 왼쪽 양조장에서 오른쪽 손님까지 이어지는 사슬 인포그래픽. 중간에 "Hotel group", "Restaurant manager", "Server" 인물 아이콘. 각 인물 위에 작은 점수판 아이콘과 "What am I measured on?" 말풍선. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: The same gap appears when an agency resells your software and is paid on signups. If nobody on their side gains when customers stay, expect fast signups and fast churn.

cards.title: Now Marco wants it exclusive.
body: Sales are strong. Marco asks that Hana sell to no other restaurant within 2 km. She already supplies three bars nearby with her regular beers.

options.text: Agree. He's her best account, and the request shows he's committed
options.feedback: She gains goodwill but loses three existing customers and any future ones nearby. She'd be betting her area on one manager who might leave.

options.text: Decline. Her beer should be available everywhere
options.feedback: She keeps her freedom, but Marco gets nothing unique for promoting her. That weakens the incentive she just worked to build.

options.text: Make the house recipe exclusive for 12 months, renewed if he hits a minimum volume
options.feedback: This is **exclusivity** done narrowly: one product, a time limit, and a condition Marco earns. He gets something special; she keeps her other accounts.

cards.title: Exclusivity is a price, not a gift.
body: **Exclusivity** is a promise not to sell to others. It has real value to the partner, so it should be paid for with commitment, such as a minimum order.

Hana shrank it three ways: *what* (one recipe), *where* (2 km), and *how long* (12 months). The volume minimum also ties back to incentives. Marco keeps the exclusive only by keeping the beer selling.

image.label: Three dials: what, where, how long
image.brief: 세 개의 다이얼 그림. "What: one recipe", "Where: 2 km", "How long: 12 months". 각 다이얼이 최대치가 아닌 낮은 쪽에 맞춰져 있음. 아래에 "Renewed if minimum volume met" 라벨.

cards.title: Incentives drift after you sign.
body: Marco might move to another hotel. Head office might change his scorecard to food waste or guest reviews. Then the deal that fit perfectly no longer fits at all.
Put a review date in the agreement, and meet the next manager early. A partnership built around one person's bonus is only as stable as that bonus.

cards.title: Now it's a house painter.
body: Luis runs a painting business. An interior designer refers her clients to him for a 10% fee, paid when the job is booked. Referrals are steady, but some clients want rushed jobs he can't do well, and complaints are rising.

options.text: Raise the fee to 15% to keep her happy
options.feedback: More money for the same behavior. She's paid for bookings, so she'll send more bookings, good fit or not.

options.text: Pay the fee after the client signs off on the finished job
options.feedback: This aligns incentives with outcomes. She now gains only when the job goes well, so she'll send clients who fit his schedule and standards.

options.text: Ask her to refer only him, in exchange for priority booking
options.feedback: Exclusivity may raise volume, but it doesn't fix why the wrong clients arrive. Fix the incentive first, then consider exclusivity.

cards.title: Design the deal for the person who decides.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Aligning incentives:** find what each decision-maker is measured on, and make the partnership help that number. **Exclusivity:** give it narrowly, for a limited time, in exchange for commitment.
**Try it today:** for one partner, write down who makes the daily choices on their side and what they are judged on. Does your deal help them win?
